full_judgment:
3. The pre-emption case was contested by the present petitioner and opposite-party No. 2 by filing a written objection in which they alleged that pre- emptor-opposite-party No.1 is not a co-sharer in the case holding. The case land appertains to SA Khatian No.18 and they have mutated their names in Mutation Case No. 717 of 1979-80 and the Jama has been separated and has been fixed at Taka 9 and accordingly, separate Khatian No.76 has been prepared in their names and they are paying rents separately. So, they claimed that the Jama and holding of the case land have been separated. Therefore, pre-emptor-opposite-party No.1 being a stranger is not entitled to pre-empt the case land. 

 4. On behalf of the pre-emptee-petitioner, the learned Counsel Mr Md Khurshid Alam Khan submitted that the learned District Judge erred in law to set aside the impugned judgment and order of the trial Court. The learned District Judge misconceived that the pre-emptor-opposite-party is not a co-sharer in the suit case, as the holding and the Jama of the case land have been separated by the Mutation Case filed by the present pre-emptee- petitioner and a separate Khatian No. 76 has been prepared in his name. So, the learned Counsel submitted that the learned District Judge did not consider Exhibit Ka which is the separate Khatian prepared by the Mutation Case No. 717 of 1979-80. So, he submitted that pre-emptor-opposite-party is not a co-sharer in the case Jote. Further he submitted that subsequently when the pre-emptor-opposite- party found it difficult to cope with her claim, she claimed the case land by way of contiguous owner. But she did not implead all the contiguous owners of the case land and has not given any boundary of the same. So, the learned Counsel submitted that the trial Court considered all these things in detail and by his judgment and order dated 14-1-2003 disallowed the pre-emption case. The learned Counsel submitted that the learned District Judge without showing any reason in support of his decision set aside the judgment and order which bears no legal value. In this regard, the learned Counsel has relied in the case of Fatema Bibi vs Manik Lal Somaddar reported in 50 DLR (AD), 97 and submitted that the Hon'ble Appellate Division in that case filed under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (Act No. XXVIII of 1951) observed that since the Khatians are different, the pre-emptor cannot be held to be a co-sharer in the case holding and as such she is not entitled to pre-emption. The learned Counsel Mr Khan submitted that the impugned judgment and order passed by the learned District Judge is not sustainable in the eye of law. 

 5. On behalf of the pre-emptor-opposite-party No.1, the learned Counsel Mr MA Kuddus Miah submitted that petitioner filed the pre-emption case on the basis of co-sharership and as kabala purchaser and also she is a contiguous owner. He submitted that in the pre-emption petition and in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in section 96 it has been mentioned that if a portion or share of a holding of a Raiyat is transferred, one or more co- sharer/tenants of the holding may, within four months of the service of notice given under section 89 of the said Act, apply to the Court for the said portion or share to be transferred to himself or themselves. He submitted that mutation Khatian does not mean the division of the holding and by mutation Khatian co-sharership does not extinguish. He submitted that the learned trial Court committed error to dismiss the pre-emption case opining that pre-emptor-opposite-party is not a co-sharer. She is a co-sharer by inheritance and by purchase: So, he submitted that the leaned Appellate Court considered all these things and allowed the pre-emption case by allowing the appeal and set aside the impugned judgment and order of the learned Joint District Judge. To substantiate his submission the learned Counsel Mr MA Kuddus Miah has relied in the case of Joynal Abedin Mollah vs Atiar Rahman reported in 2 BCR (AD), 431 and submitted that the holding of the case land has not been separated by the separation of the Jama. So, the learned Counsel submitted that the impugned judgment and order passed by the learned District Judge needs no interference by this Court. Accordingly, the Rule is liable to be discharged. 

 6. We have perused the impugned judgment and order of both the Courts below together with the miscellaneous application and written-objection and the exhibited documents filed by the parties in this miscellaneous case. It is found that by Exhibit Ka a separate Khatian has been prepared in the name of Nawab Ali at a Jama of Taka 9 in Mutation Case No.717 of 1979-80. That Khatian was approved by the then Circle Officer (Revenue), Barura, on 15-4- 1980 and since then Nawab Ali is paying rents as per his separate Khatian. Now, what would be the implication of this mutation case in the original Khatian and holding? In the case of Fatema Bibi vs Manik Lal Samaddar and others their Lordships of the Appellate Division held that when the Khatians are different, the pre-emptor cannot be held to be a co-sharer in the case holding and not entitled to pre- emption. This decision of the Hon'ble Appellate Division was given in a case filed under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. In paragraph No. 6 of this case the Hon'ble Appellate Division has given the detailed observation which runs as follows: 

 "It appears that pre-emption was sought for in respect of 0.05 acres of land in plot No.991 under SA Khatian No.185, whereas the pre- emptor purchased land from Plot No. 99l appertaining to separate SA Khatian No.179 and, as such, she was not a tenant in the case holding. The Lower Appellate Court found that the pre- emptor was not a tenant of the case holding No.185, whereas the respondents were co- sharers by purchase. Hence, Lower Appellate Court rightly held that the pre-emptor had no locus standi to file the pre-emption case in respect of land of SA Khatian No.185. In both the Khatians plot No.991 is a common plot, but pre-emptor being not a co-sharer in SA Khatian No.185 it was rightly held by the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division that the application is not maintainable. The learned Single Judge also affirmed the finding of the Lower Appellate Court that the land in question being non-agricultural in nature, the application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was not maintainable. The learned Single Judge having correctly decided the point of maintainability of the application for Pre- emption the same calls for no interference." 

 7. In the case of Alfazuddin Ahmed vs Abdur Rahman reported in 8 MLR (AD) 153 = 55 DLR(AD) 108 their Lordships held that separation of tenancy/Jama Khatian disentitled the petitioner from the right of pre-emption. Co-sharership in a tenancy of non-agricultural land ceases through two different ways one is partition of land and the other is separation of the tenancy by splitting up the Jama Khatian. Though this case was under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, but the principles laid down therein are the same. The learned District Judge failed to consider the implication of the separation of the Jama and preparation of separate Khatian in the name of the present petitioner and on erroneous view be set aside the impugned judgment and order of the Joint District Judge and allowed the pre-emption case. In the deed of transfer the scheduled land has been shown by mentioning the old Khatian and holding, but the purchaser-pre-emptee after his purchase separated the Jama and the Khatian as per the aforesaid mutation case and by opening separate Khatian in his name. So, we find that the holding has been separated and the pre- emptor-opposite-party cannot claim pre-emption of the case land. Lastly, the pre-emptor-opposite-party rested her claim on the contiguous owner. But no schedule of the case land has been furnished and in the pre-emption case none of the contiguous owners has been made party. Therefore, her subsequent claim as a contiguous owner also fails. Under such circumstances we find merit in the Rule.
